ambaṣṭha
------------------------------------------
When the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् was born in the Hindu society, the seed of admixture of castes was also sown. Even as early as the महाभारत period, such admixture (varṇasaṅkara) was deplored. One of the several castes born out of such admixture is the अम्बष्ठ, the offspring of a ब्राह्मण ड़थेर् and a वैश्य मोथेर्. Practice of medicine and surgery as also agriculture are the professions recommended for this caste. Some books make the अम्बष्ठ the offspring of a क्षत्त्रिय ड़थेर् from a वैश्य मोथेर्. Fighting is the vocation recommended.
Ambaṣṭha seems to be the name of a country also. A king, Āmbaṣṭhya, is said to have performed अश्वमेध sacrifice (vide ऐतरेय Brāhmaṇa 39.7). Mahā-bhārata mentions another king अम्बष्ठ who fought on the side of the Kauravas and met his death at the hands of अर्जुन. कṁस’s mahout who tried to assassinate बलराम and कृष्ण was also known as अम्बष्ठ.

Ambā
(‘mother’)
------------------------------------------
Though a general word, meaning ‘mother,’ it is more often used as a proper noun, as a name of one of the aspects of पार्वती, the divine spouse of Lord शिव. Said to be of the colour of water lily, she is depicted with four hands, carrying पाश (noose), पद्म (lotus) and pātra (vessel) in three hands whereas the fourth one is exhibiting the abhayamudrā (pose assuring freedom from fear).
Mother दुर्गा is also sometimes called अम्बा.
The first daughter of the king of काशी was also named अम्बा. अम्बिका and Ambālikā were her sisters. भीष्म brought the three sisters by force during their स्वयṁवर. When he learnt that अम्बा had already been betrothed to the king Saubha, he sent her to him. However the king Saubha refused to accept her. She returned and pressed भीष्म himself to marry her. He refused her request since he had vowed to remain celibate. Incensed by this, she performed austerities to kill भीष्म, was reborn as Śikhaṇḍī (an offspring of Drupada) and ultimately killed him in the महाभारत war.

Ambikā
------------------------------------------
An aspect of goddess पार्वती, अम्बिका is described as being seated on a lion. She has three eyes and is adorned with various ornaments. Out of her four hands, three hold दर्पण (mirror), खड्ग (sword) and खेटक (shield). The fourth (one of the right hands) exhibits the varadamudrā (boon-giving pose).
In the Mahābhārata, अम्बिका was the wife of Vicitravīrya and मोथेर् of the blind king धृतराष्ट्र. Ambālikā, her sister, was another wife who became the मोथेर् of पाण्डु.

Ambarīṣa
------------------------------------------
Ambarīṣa was an emperor belonging to the Sūryavaṁśa and the इक्ष्वाकु lineage. A worthy son of a worthy ड़थेर् (Māndhātṛ), अम्बरीष was deeply devoted to Lord विष्णु. He was very meticulous in observing the fast on ekādaśīs (11th day after new-मोओन् or full-मोओन्, on which day ड़स्तिन्ग् is obligatory). दुर्वासस्, a sage known for his short temper, once attemp-ted to make him swerve from the rules of the ritual but failed in his efforts. Actually the tables were turned against him. The सुदर्शनचक्र (discus of Lord विष्णु) pursued him relentlessly until he had to seek the forgiveness and deliverance from the king अम्बरीष himself. (For details see Bhāgavatam 9.4, 5.)
There was another अम्बरीष, the son of Nābhāga. He was known for his generosity and devotion.
In the Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa, 61) we come across yet another अम्बरीष who lost the yajñapaśu (the sacrificial animal) during the conduct of a sacrifice and was advised to substitute the lost animal with a human being. शुनश्शेफ, the middle son of a sage ऋचीक, was purchased for this purpose. But the boy was ultimately saved by the dynamic sage विश्वामित्र.
Śunaśśepha’s story appears in some पुराणस् with variations in which Hariś-चन्द्र is the king and not अम्बरीष.
The Mahābhārata contains an Ambarīṣa-गीता (Anugītā-parva, 12). After attaining perfection अम्बरीष teaches that लोभ (greed) is a great enemy responsible for spiritual disaster, and hence it must be rooted out.

Ambuvācī
(‘expecting rains’)
------------------------------------------
Mother Earth (Bhūdevī or Dharaṇī) when expecting the rains (i.e. just before the starting of the rainy season), is called ‘Ambuvācī’. It is also the name of the fertility rite normally observed in Bengal. During this period of four days—Āṣāḍha कृष्ण daśamī to trayodaśī (June/July)—the मोथेर् Earth is said to be unclean and hence no ploughing or sowing or any other type of farm work is done.
